items.stem: What is the charge on the ion formed by an element in group 16?
items.markingKey: D. Gains two electrons to complete an octet.

items.stem: Explain why a chloride ion is larger than a chlorine atom.
items.answer: The extra electron increases electron–electron repulsion in the outer shell while the nuclear charge is unchanged, so the electron cloud expands.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The extra electron increases electron–electron repulsion in the outer shell while the nuclear charge is unchanged, so the electron cloud expands. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Why do noble gases rarely form ions?
options: They have no electrons in the outer shell.
They have full outer shells and very high ionisation energies.
items.answer: They have full outer shells and very high ionisation energies.
items.markingKey: B. Stable configurations; high IE.

items.stem: Which species is isoelectronic with O²⁻?
items.answer: N³⁻
items.markingKey: D. O²⁻ and N³⁻ both have 10 electrons.

items.stem: Describe, in terms of electrons, the formation of the ionic compound between lithium (Z = 3) and bromine (Z = 35), giving the electron configurations of the ions and the formula of the compound.
items.answer: Each Li loses 1 electron(s) → Li⁺ ([He]); each Br gains 1 → Br⁻ ([Kr]); LiBr; ions held by electrostatic attraction in a lattice.
items.markingKey: Electron transfer from Li to Br with correct numbers (1); configurations [He] and [Kr] (1); formula LiBr (1); electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in a lattice (1).

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The octet rule is a reliable way to predict the charges on ions."
items.answer: Useful for main-group elements but limited; charge depends on the balance of ionisation energies and lattice enthalpy.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: correctly predicts charges for groups 1, 2, 13, 15–17; simple and quick. Arguments against: transition metals form ions with variable charges that do not have octets (Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺); heavier p-block metals (Pb²⁺, Sn²⁺) do not follow it; energetics (IE vs lattice enthalpy) are the real explanation. Supported judgement: Useful for main-group elements but limited; charge depends on the balance of ionisation energies and lattice enthalpy.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "cation"?
options: The simplest ratio of ions in an ionic compound, used because ionic compounds have no molecules
A giant three-dimensional regular arrangement of alternating cations and anions held together by electrostatic attraction
A positively charged ion, formed when an atom loses one or more electrons
The radius of an ion in an ionic lattice; cations are smaller and anions larger than their parent atoms
items.answer: A positively charged ion, formed when an atom loses one or more electrons
items.markingKey: C. "cation" is a positively charged ion, formed when an atom loses one or more electrons.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A positively charged ion, formed when an atom loses one or more electrons"?
items.answer: cation
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of cation.

items.stem: Sana writes: "Ionic bonds form because sodium wants to lose an electron." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Atoms have no desires; the overall process is energetically favourable because the lattice energy released when oppositely charged ions attract outweighs the energy needed to form the ions.
items.markingKey: Atoms have no desires; the overall process is energetically favourable because the lattice energy released when oppositely charged ions attract outweighs the energy needed to form the ions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between an anion and a cation.
items.answer: A cation is positive, formed by losing electrons (usually metals); an anion is negative, formed by gaining electrons (usually non-metals).
items.markingKey: A cation is positive, formed by losing electrons (usually metals); an anion is negative, formed by gaining electrons (usually non-metals). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why the ions in the series O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺, Mg²⁺ decrease in radius.
items.answer: They are isoelectronic (10 electrons); nuclear charge increases from 8 to 12, so the same electrons are pulled closer to the nucleus.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They are isoelectronic (10 electrons); nuclear charge increases from 8 to 12, so the same electrons are pulled closer to the nucleus. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "An ionic bond is the transfer of electrons from a metal to a non-metal." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Electron transfer forms the ions; the ionic bond itself is the electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions.
items.markingKey: Electron transfer forms the ions; the ionic bond itself is the electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Which shows the ions in order of decreasing ionic radius?
items.answer: N³⁻ > O²⁻ > F⁻ > Mg²⁺
items.markingKey: C. Isoelectronic ions: radius falls as nuclear charge rises (N³⁻ 146 pm, O²⁻ 140 pm, F⁻ 133 pm, Mg²⁺ 72 pm).

items.stem: Describe, in terms of electrons, the formation of the ionic compound between calcium (Z = 20) and nitrogen (Z = 7), giving the electron configurations of the ions and the formula of the compound.
items.answer: Each Ca loses 2 electron(s) → Ca²⁺ ([Ar]); each N gains 3 → N³⁻ ([Ne]); Ca₃N₂; ions held by electrostatic attraction in a lattice.
items.markingKey: Electron transfer from Ca to N with correct numbers (1); configurations [Ar] and [Ne] (1); formula Ca₃N₂ (1); electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in a lattice (1).

items.stem: Which species is isoelectronic with Ne?
items.answer: Na⁺
items.markingKey: D. Ne and Na⁺ both have 10 electrons.

items.stem: Describe, in terms of electrons, the formation of the ionic compound between caesium (Z = 55) and nitrogen (Z = 7), giving the electron configurations of the ions and the formula of the compound.
items.answer: Each Cs loses 1 electron(s) → Cs⁺ (); each N gains 3 → N³⁻ ([Ne]); Cs₃N; ions held by electrostatic attraction in a lattice.
items.markingKey: Electron transfer from Cs to N with correct numbers (1); configurations  and [Ne] (1); formula Cs₃N (1); electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in a lattice (1).

items.stem: A student claims: "Ionic bonds form because sodium wants to lose an electron." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Atoms have no desires; the overall process is energetically favourable because the lattice energy released when oppositely charged ions attract outweighs the energy needed to form the ions.
items.markingKey: Atoms have no desires; the overall process is energetically favourable because the lattice energy released when oppositely charged ions attract outweighs the energy needed to form the ions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Potassium reacts with fluorine to form an ionic compound. (a) Deduce its formula. (b) State the total number of electrons transferred per formula unit. (c) Explain, using the successive ionisation energies of K, why it forms a 1+ ion. (d) Predict, with a reason, whether its melting point is higher or lower than that of sodium chloride.
items.answer: (a) KF; (b) 1; (d) similar/lower
items.markingKey: (a) KF (A1). (b) 1 electrons (A1). (c) a large jump after the first IE: the next electron would come from an inner shell (R1). (d) similar or lower depending on ion sizes; same charges, compare radii (R1).

items.stem: Calcium (Z = 20) reacts with nitrogen (Z = 7) when heated. (a) Give the electron configurations of the atoms and ions involved. (b) Deduce the formula of the product, explaining how the charges balance. (c) Explain why the product has a high melting point.
items.answer: (a) Ca [Ar] 4s² → Ca²⁺ [Ar]; N [He] 2s² 2p³ → N³⁻ [Ne]. (b) Ca₃N₂: 3 × (+2) = 2 × (−3) = 6 electrons transferred. (c) Giant ionic lattice with strong electrostatic attraction between highly charged ions; much energy is needed to separate them.
items.markingKey: (a) Ca [Ar] 4s² → Ca²⁺ [Ar]; N [He] 2s² 2p³ → N³⁻ [Ne]. (b) Ca₃N₂: 3 × (+2) = 2 × (−3) = 6 electrons transferred. (c) Giant ionic lattice with strong electrostatic attraction between highly charged ions; much energy is needed to separate them.

items.stem: Lithium reacts with oxygen to form lithium oxide. Describe the formation of lithium oxide in terms of electron transfer, draw the electron arrangements (dot-and-cross) of the ions and explain why the compound conducts electricity only when molten.
items.answer: 2Li → 2Li⁺ + 2e⁻; O + 2e⁻ → O²⁻; Li₂O. Dot-and-cross: [Li]⁺ with empty outer shell (shown as 1s²), [O]²⁻ with 8 outer electrons (six dots, two crosses), square brackets with charges. Solid: ions fixed; molten: ions mobile and carry charge.
items.markingKey: 2Li → 2Li⁺ + 2e⁻; O + 2e⁻ → O²⁻; Li₂O. Dot-and-cross: [Li]⁺ with empty outer shell (shown as 1s²), [O]²⁻ with 8 outer electrons (six dots, two crosses), square brackets with charges. Solid: ions fixed; molten: ions mobile and carry charge.

items.stem: What is the formula of ammonium phosphate?
items.answer: (NH₄)₃PO₄
items.markingKey: D. Three NH₄⁺ balance PO₄³⁻.

items.stem: Which pair of names and formulae is correct?
items.answer: sodium sulfite, Na₂SO₃
items.markingKey: B. Sulfite SO₃²⁻ needs two Na⁺.

items.stem: A student claims: "The formula of aluminium sulfate is AlSO₄." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Al³⁺ and SO₄²⁻ must balance: Al₂(SO₄)₃.
items.markingKey: Al³⁺ and SO₄²⁻ must balance: Al₂(SO₄)₃. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Write the formula of the ionic compound magnesium nitrite, showing how the charges balance.
items.answer: Mg(NO₂)₂
items.markingKey: Ions Mg²⁺ and NO₂⁻ (1); charges balance in Mg(NO₂)₂ (1).

items.stem: What is the formula of magnesium nitride?
items.answer: Mg₃N₂
items.markingKey: C. Mg²⁺ and N³⁻: Mg₃N₂ is neutral.

State the formula, including charge, of the sulfite ion.
items.answer: SO₃²⁻
items.markingKey: SO₃²⁻ – formula and charge both required (1).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The simplest ratio of ions in an ionic compound, used because ionic compounds have no molecules"?
items.answer: formula unit

items.stem: Distinguish between nitrate and nitrite.
items.answer: Nitrite is NO₂⁻ and nitrate is NO₃⁻; the “-ate” ion has more oxygen.
items.markingKey: Nitrite is NO₂⁻ and nitrate is NO₃⁻; the “-ate” ion has more oxygen. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why the formula of an ionic compound must be electrically neutral.
items.answer: The compound as a whole has no net charge; the total positive charge of the cations must equal the total negative charge of the anions, which fixes the ratio of ions.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The compound as a whole has no net charge; the total positive charge of the cations must equal the total negative charge of the anions, which fixes the ratio of ions. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Which compound contains the nitride ion?
items.answer: Mg₃N₂
items.markingKey: B. Nitride = N³⁻.

items.stem: Which ion has a 3− charge?
items.answer: phosphate
items.markingKey: A. PO₄³⁻.

items.stem: Jonas writes: "Magnesium hydroxide is MgOH₂." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Brackets are needed: Mg(OH)₂; MgOH₂ would mean one O and two H atoms.
items.markingKey: Brackets are needed: Mg(OH)₂; MgOH₂ would mean one O and two H atoms. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Write the formula of the ionic compound zinc sulfite, showing how the charges balance.
items.answer: ZnSO₃
items.markingKey: Ions Zn²⁺ and SO₃²⁻ (1); charges balance in ZnSO₃ (1).

items.stem: What is the formula of iron(II) ethanoate?
items.answer: (CH₃COO)₂Fe
items.markingKey: D. Fe²⁺ and CH₃COO⁻: (CH₃COO)₂Fe is neutral.

items.stem: Name the compound Na₂CO₃.
items.answer: sodium carbonate
items.markingKey: sodium carbonate (1).

items.stem: Write the formula of the ionic compound silver nitrate, showing how the charges balance.
items.answer: AgNO₃
items.markingKey: Ions Ag⁺ and NO₃⁻ (1); charges balance in AgNO₃ (1).

items.stem: "Memorising the formulae of polyatomic ions is unnecessary because they can be looked up." Discuss.
items.answer: Knowing the common ions is an essential working vocabulary even if reference sources exist.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: data booklets and references are always available in practice; understanding charge balance matters more. Arguments against: fluency speeds up all stoichiometry and equation writing; recognising ions is needed to interpret names, labels and experimental observations. Supported judgement: Knowing the common ions is an essential working vocabulary even if reference sources exist. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: A fertiliser label lists “ammonium phosphate” and “potassium nitrate”. (a) Write the formula of each compound. (b) Calculate the percentage by mass of nitrogen in each. (c) Suggest which is the better source of nitrogen per kilogram.
items.answer: (a) (NH₄)₃PO₄ and KNO₃. (b) (NH₄)₃PO₄: 3 × 14.01/149.12 × 100 = 28.2 %; KNO₃: 14.01/101.11 × 100 = 13.9 %. (c) ammonium phosphate – about twice the nitrogen content per kg (and it also supplies phosphorus).
items.markingKey: (a) (NH₄)₃PO₄ and KNO₃. (b) (NH₄)₃PO₄: 3 × 14.01/149.12 × 100 = 28.2 %; KNO₃: 14.01/101.11 × 100 = 13.9 %. (c) ammonium phosphate – about twice the nitrogen content per kg (and it also supplies phosphorus).

items.stem: Aqueous copper(II) sulfate is mixed with aqueous sodium hydroxide and a precipitate (blue) forms. (a) Write the formulae of the two reactants. (b) Identify the precipitate and write an ionic equation, with state symbols, for its formation. (c) Identify the spectator ions. (d) Name the salt left in solution.
items.answer: (a) CuSO₄, NaOH; (b) Cu(OH)₂: Cu²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Cu(OH)₂(s); (c) Na⁺ and SO₄²⁻; (d) sodium sulfate
items.markingKey: (a) CuSO₄ and NaOH (A1). (b) Cu(OH)₂ (A1); Cu²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Cu(OH)₂(s) – balanced with state symbols (A1). (c) Na⁺ and SO₄²⁻ (A1). (d) sodium sulfate, Na₂SO₄ (A1).

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "coordination number".
items.answer: The number of nearest oppositely charged ions surrounding a given ion in a lattice (6 in NaCl)
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the number of nearest oppositely charged ions surrounding a given ion in a lattice (6 in NaCl). Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: The lattice enthalpy of NaBr is 754 kJ mol⁻¹ and that of NaI is 705 kJ mol⁻¹. Explain this difference.
items.answer: Stronger electrostatic attraction in NaBr: the ions in NaBr are smaller (sum of radii 298 pm vs 322 pm) with the same charges.
items.markingKey: the ions in NaBr are smaller (sum of radii 298 pm vs 322 pm) with the same charges (1); ions closer together / greater charge density gives stronger electrostatic attraction (1); more energy needed to separate the ions (1).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why many ionic compounds dissolve in water but not in hexane.
items.answer: Polar water molecules are attracted to the ions (ion–dipole attractions), releasing energy that helps overcome the lattice; non-polar hexane cannot interact strongly with ions. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Polar water molecules are attracted to the ions (ion–dipole attractions), releasing energy that helps overcome the lattice; non-polar hexane cannot interact strongly with ions. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Substance X has the following properties: melting point 1080 °C; does not conduct when solid; conducts when molten and when dissolved; brittle. Deduce the type of bonding and structure in X, giving reasons based on two properties.
items.answer: ionic
items.markingKey: ionic (1); two properties correctly linked to structure (e.g. conduction only when ions/electrons mobile, melting point reflecting strength of forces) (2).

items.stem: Predict which of NaCl and LiCl has the higher melting point, giving a reason.
items.answer: LiCl: smaller ions (shorter distance between ion centres) (lattice enthalpies 864 vs 790 kJ mol⁻¹).
items.markingKey: LiCl (1); reason in terms of ionic charge/radius and strength of electrostatic attraction (1).

items.stem:
The table shows the sum of ionic radii and the lattice enthalpy for several compounds.

compound | r(cation) + r(anion) / pm | lattice enthalpy / kJ mol⁻¹
LiCl | 257 | 864
NaCl | 283 | 790
KCl | 319 | 720

(a) Describe the trend shown. (b) Explain the trend in terms of electrostatic attraction. (c) Predict, with a reason, how the lattice enthalpy of a compound with ions of double the charge but the same radii would compare.
items.answer: (a) lattice enthalpy decreases as the sum of radii increases; (c) roughly four times larger
items.markingKey: (a) larger distance → smaller lattice enthalpy (A1). (b) force ∝ product of charges / distance; ions further apart attract less strongly, less energy needed to separate (R1 R1). (c) charge product ×4, so roughly four times larger (e.g. MgO vs NaF) (R1).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "coordination number"?
options: The simplest ratio of ions in an ionic compound, used because ionic compounds have no molecules
The standard enthalpy change when one mole of a solid ionic compound is separated into its gaseous ions; it is endothermic, e.g. NaCl(s) → Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g)
The oxidation state of a metal that can form ions of different charge, e.g. iron(III) = Fe³⁺
The number of nearest oppositely charged ions surrounding a given ion in a lattice (6 in NaCl)
items.answer: The number of nearest oppositely charged ions surrounding a given ion in a lattice (6 in NaCl)
items.markingKey: D. "coordination number" is the number of nearest oppositely charged ions surrounding a given ion in a lattice (6 in NaCl).

items.stem: Under which conditions does sodium chloride conduct electricity?
options: when molten or dissolved in water
only as a solid at high pressure
items.answer: when molten or dissolved in water
items.markingKey: C. Ions must be mobile.

items.stem: Which explains why KCl has a lower lattice enthalpy than NaCl?
items.answer: K⁺ is larger than Na⁺.
items.markingKey: D. Larger ions → weaker attraction.

items.stem: A student claims: "Lattice enthalpy is the energy released when one mole of a solid is formed from its elements." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: That is the enthalpy of formation; lattice enthalpy (IB definition) is the endothermic change for separating 1 mol of solid into gaseous ions.
items.markingKey: That is the enthalpy of formation; lattice enthalpy (IB definition) is the endothermic change for separating 1 mol of solid into gaseous ions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between the volatility of simple molecular compounds and the volatility of ionic compounds.
items.answer: Ionic compounds have low volatility (high boiling points) because strong ionic bonds throughout the lattice must be broken; simple molecular compounds are volatile because only weak intermolecular forces must be overcome.
items.markingKey: Ionic compounds have low volatility (high boiling points) because strong ionic bonds throughout the lattice must be broken; simple molecular compounds are volatile because only weak intermolecular forces must be overcome. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity but molten sodium chloride does.
items.answer: In the solid the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice and cannot move; when molten the lattice breaks down and the ions are free to move and carry charge.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: In the solid the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice and cannot move; when molten the lattice breaks down and the ions are free to move and carry charge. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Which compound has the largest lattice enthalpy?
items.answer: MgF₂
items.markingKey: B. Lattice enthalpy increases with ionic charge and decreases with ionic radius: KI 650, MgCl₂ 2540, MgF₂ 2978, NaBr 754 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.stem: Which statement about magnesium sulfate dissolved in water is correct?
options: It conducts because it has delocalised electrons.
It does not conduct because its ions are fixed in a lattice.
It conducts because its ions are free to move.
It does not conduct because it contains no charged particles.
items.answer: It conducts because its ions are free to move.
items.markingKey: C. Conduction requires mobile charged particles; ionic compounds conduct only when molten or in solution.

items.stem: Which statement about copper(II) sulfate solid is correct?
options: It does not conduct because it contains no ions.
It conducts because it contains ions.
It conducts because electrons move through the lattice.
It does not conduct because its ions are fixed in position.
items.answer: It does not conduct because its ions are fixed in position.
items.markingKey: D. Conduction requires mobile charged particles; ionic compounds conduct only when molten or in solution.

items.stem: A student claims: "Sodium chloride conducts electricity when solid because it contains charged particles." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Ions are present but fixed in the lattice; conduction requires mobile charge carriers, so the solid does not conduct.
items.markingKey: Ions are present but fixed in the lattice; conduction requires mobile charge carriers, so the solid does not conduct. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Which compound has the smallest lattice enthalpy?
items.answer: NaBr
items.markingKey: B. Lattice enthalpy increases with ionic charge and decreases with ionic radius: NaBr 754, NaF 930, LiCl 864, CaCl₂ 2271 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The ionic model fully explains the properties of all compounds of metals with non-metals."
items.answer: The ionic model works for compounds with a large electronegativity difference but must be extended for polarising cations and polarisable anions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: explains high melting points, brittleness and conductivity when molten for NaCl, MgO; lattice enthalpy trends follow charge and radius. Arguments against: AlCl₃ sublimes at 180 °C and exists as Al₂Cl₆ molecules – covalent character; experimental lattice enthalpies differ from purely ionic theoretical values when polarisation occurs (e.g. AgCl); some metal–non-metal compounds are semiconductors. Supported judgement: The ionic model works for compounds with a large electronegativity difference but must be extended for polarising cations and polarisable anions. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: Design an experiment to show that a white solid is ionic. Describe the tests, the expected observations and the reasoning.
items.answer: Test melting point (high, e.g. > 500 °C); test conductivity of solid (none), molten or aqueous (conducts – ions mobile); solubility in water vs hexane (dissolves in water); electrolysis of molten/aqueous sample gives products at electrodes. Together these indicate a giant ionic lattice.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the names sulfide, sulfite and sulfate refer to different ions.
items.answer: Sulfide is S²⁻ (no oxygen); sulfite is SO₃²⁻ and sulfate SO₄²⁻, oxyanions with more oxygen giving the “-ate” ending, so the suffix encodes composition.

items.stem: Explain why magnesium forms Mg²⁺ ions rather than Mg⁺ or Mg³⁺ ions.
items.answer: Losing the two 3s electrons gives the stable [Ne] configuration; removing a third electron would require breaking into the inner 2p shell, which needs far more energy (very large third ionisation energy).

items.stem: The lattice enthalpy of CaCl₂ is 2271 kJ mol⁻¹ and that of KCl is 720 kJ mol⁻¹. Explain this difference.
items.answer: Stronger electrostatic attraction in CaCl₂: the ions in CaCl₂ carry higher charges (Ca²⁺, Cl⁻) and are smaller.
items.markingKey: the ions in CaCl₂ carry higher charges (Ca²⁺, Cl⁻) and are smaller (1); ions closer together / greater charge density gives stronger electrostatic attraction (1); more energy needed to separate the ions (1).

items.stem: Aluminium (group 13) reacts with sulfur (group 16). State the charges on the ions formed and deduce the formula of the compound.
items.answer: Al³⁺ and S²⁻; Al₂S₃
items.markingKey: Charges from group numbers (1); formula balanced for neutrality: Al₂S₃ (1).

items.stem: Ingrid writes: "The formula of aluminium sulfate is AlSO₄." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Al³⁺ and SO₄²⁻ must balance: Al₂(SO₄)₃.
items.markingKey: Al³⁺ and SO₄²⁻ must balance: Al₂(SO₄)₃. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Predict which of NaF and KF has the higher melting point, giving a reason.
items.answer: NaF: smaller ions (shorter distance between ion centres) (lattice enthalpies 930 vs 829 kJ mol⁻¹).
items.markingKey: NaF (1); reason in terms of ionic charge/radius and strength of electrostatic attraction (1).

items.stem: Which species is isoelectronic with Al³⁺?
items.answer: N³⁻
items.markingKey: C. Al³⁺ and N³⁻ both have 10 electrons.

items.stem: Deduce the formula of magnesium sulfite.
items.answer: MgSO₃
items.markingKey: Ions Mg²⁺ and SO₃²⁻ (1); charges balance in MgSO₃ (1).

items.stem: Substance W has the following properties: melting point 1710 °C; does not conduct in any state; insoluble in all solvents; very hard. Deduce the type of bonding and structure in W, giving reasons based on two properties.
items.answer: giant covalent (covalent network)
items.markingKey: giant covalent (covalent network) (1); two properties correctly linked to structure (e.g. conduction only when ions/electrons mobile, melting point reflecting strength of forces) (2).

items.stem: A student claims: "An ionic bond is the transfer of electrons from a metal to a non-metal." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Electron transfer forms the ions; the ionic bond itself is the electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions.
items.markingKey: Electron transfer forms the ions; the ionic bond itself is the electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: (a) Write the formula of chromium(III) sulfate. (b) Calculate its molar mass. (c) Calculate the total amount of ions, in mol, in 5.00 g of the compound. (d) Calculate the number of oxygen atoms in this sample.
"The ionic model fully explains the properties of all compounds of metals with non-metals." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: The ionic model works for compounds with a large electronegativity difference but must be extended for polarising cations and polarisable anions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: explains high melting points, brittleness and conductivity when molten for NaCl, MgO; lattice enthalpy trends follow charge and radius. Arguments against: AlCl₃ sublimes at 180 °C and exists as Al₂Cl₆ molecules – covalent character; experimental lattice enthalpies differ from purely ionic theoretical values when polarisation occurs (e.g. AgCl); some metal–non-metal compounds are semiconductors. Supported judgement: The ionic model works for compounds with a large electronegativity difference but must be extended for polarising cations and polarisable anions. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: Aluminium reacts with oxygen to form an ionic compound. (a) Deduce its formula. (b) State the total number of electrons transferred per formula unit. (c) Explain, using the successive ionisation energies of Al, why it forms a 3+ ion. (d) Predict, with a reason, whether its melting point is higher or lower than that of sodium chloride.
items.answer: (a) Al₂O₃; (b) 6; (d) higher
items.markingKey: (a) Al₂O₃ (A1). (b) 6 electrons (A1). (c) a large jump after the third IE: the next electron would come from an inner shell (R1). (d) higher: ions carry greater charge(s) so stronger electrostatic attraction (R1).

items.stem: "Memorising the formulae of polyatomic ions is unnecessary because they can be looked up." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Knowing the common ions is an essential working vocabulary even if reference sources exist.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: data booklets and references are always available in practice; understanding charge balance matters more. Arguments against: fluency speeds up all stoichiometry and equation writing; recognising ions is needed to interpret names, labels and experimental observations. Supported judgement: Knowing the common ions is an essential working vocabulary even if reference sources exist. Markbands (12 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions"?
items.answer: ionic bond
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of ionic bond.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Roman numeral in a name"?
options: An ion made of two or more covalently bonded atoms carrying an overall charge, such as SO₄²⁻ or NH₄⁺
The oxidation state of a metal that can form ions of different charge, e.g. iron(III) = Fe³⁺
The tendency of an ionic solid to shatter when a force displaces layers so that ions of like charge come next to each other and repel
The radius of an ion in an ionic lattice; cations are smaller and anions larger than their parent atoms
items.answer: The oxidation state of a metal that can form ions of different charge, e.g. iron(III) = Fe³⁺
items.markingKey: B. "Roman numeral in a name" is the oxidation state of a metal that can form ions of different charge, e.g. iron(III) = Fe³⁺.

items.stem: Why do ionic compounds have high melting points?
items.answer: Many strong electrostatic attractions between ions in the lattice must be overcome.
items.markingKey: Many strong electrostatic attractions between ions in the lattice must be overcome. Giant lattice.

items.stem: Which atom forms an ion that is larger than the atom?
items.answer: sulfur
items.markingKey: B. Anions are larger than their atoms.

items.stem: Briefly explain why Roman numerals are used in the names of compounds of transition elements such as copper.
items.answer: Transition elements form ions with more than one possible charge (Cu⁺ and Cu²⁺); the Roman numeral states the oxidation state, so the formula is unambiguous.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Transition elements form ions with more than one possible charge (Cu⁺ and Cu²⁺); the Roman numeral states the oxidation state, so the formula is unambiguous. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why ionic compounds are brittle.
items.answer: A force can shift layers of ions so that ions of the same charge come next to each other; the repulsion between like charges causes the lattice to split.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A force can shift layers of ions so that ions of the same charge come next to each other; the repulsion between like charges causes the lattice to split. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between a cation and an anion.
items.answer: A cation is positive, formed by losing electrons (usually metals); an anion is negative, formed by gaining electrons (usually non-metals).
items.markingKey: A cation is positive, formed by losing electrons (usually metals); an anion is negative, formed by gaining electrons (usually non-metals). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: What is the charge of the metal ion in Cu₂O?
items.markingKey: C. O²⁻ balanced by two Cu⁺.

items.stem: The lattice enthalpy of MgF₂ is 2978 kJ mol⁻¹ and that of NaBr is 754 kJ mol⁻¹. Explain this difference.
items.answer: Stronger electrostatic attraction in MgF₂: the ions in MgF₂ carry higher charges (Mg²⁺, F⁻) and are smaller.
items.markingKey: the ions in MgF₂ carry higher charges (Mg²⁺, F⁻) and are smaller (1); ions closer together / greater charge density gives stronger electrostatic attraction (1); more energy needed to separate the ions (1).

items.stem: Which species is isoelectronic with F⁻?
items.answer: N³⁻
items.markingKey: A. F⁻ and N³⁻ both have 10 electrons.

items.stem: "Magnesium hydroxide is MgOH₂." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Brackets are needed: Mg(OH)₂; MgOH₂ would mean one O and two H atoms.
items.markingKey: Brackets are needed: Mg(OH)₂; MgOH₂ would mean one O and two H atoms. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Substance V has the following properties: melting point 714 °C; solid does not conduct; aqueous solution conducts. Deduce the type of bonding and structure in V, giving reasons based on two properties.
items.answer: ionic
items.markingKey: ionic (1); two properties correctly linked to structure (e.g. conduction only when ions/electrons mobile, melting point reflecting strength of forces) (2).

items.stem: Describe, in terms of electrons, the formation of the ionic compound between magnesium (Z = 12) and selenium (Z = 34), giving the electron configurations of the ions and the formula of the compound.
items.answer: Each Mg loses 2 electron(s) → Mg²⁺ ([Ne]); each Se gains 2 → Se²⁻ ([Kr]); MgSe; ions held by electrostatic attraction in a lattice.
items.markingKey: Electron transfer from Mg to Se with correct numbers (1); configurations [Ne] and [Kr] (1); formula MgSe (1); electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in a lattice (1).

items.stem: Deduce the formula of manganese(II) nitride.
items.answer: Mn₃N₂
items.markingKey: Ions Mn²⁺ and N³⁻ (1); charges balance in Mn₃N₂ (1).

items.stem: Using ionic charges and radii, deduce whether NaF or NaBr has the greater lattice enthalpy.
items.answer: NaF: smaller ions (shorter distance between ion centres) (lattice enthalpies 930 vs 754 kJ mol⁻¹).
items.markingKey: NaF (1); reason in terms of ionic charge/radius and strength of electrostatic attraction (1).

items.stem: Describe, in terms of electrons, the formation of the ionic compound between aluminium (Z = 13) and fluorine (Z = 9), giving the electron configurations of the ions and the formula of the compound.
items.answer: Each Al loses 3 electron(s) → Al³⁺ ([Ne]); each F gains 1 → F⁻ ([Ne]); AlF₃; ions held by electrostatic attraction in a lattice.
items.markingKey: Electron transfer from Al to F with correct numbers (1); configurations [Ne] and [Ne] (1); formula AlF₃ (1); electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in a lattice (1).

items.stem: (a) Write the formula of barium phosphate. (b) Calculate its molar mass. (c) Calculate the total amount of ions, in mol, in 10.00 g of the compound. (d) Calculate the number of oxygen atoms in this sample.
"Lattice enthalpy alone determines whether an ionic compound is soluble in water." Discuss.
items.answer: Solubility depends on the balance of lattice and hydration enthalpies and entropy, not lattice enthalpy alone.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: high lattice enthalpy compounds (MgO, CaF₂) tend to be insoluble; lattice must be broken for dissolving. Arguments against: hydration enthalpies of the ions are equally important; entropy changes contribute to ΔG of solution; many compounds with high lattice enthalpy are still soluble (e.g. MgSO₄). Supported judgement: Solubility depends on the balance of lattice and hydration enthalpies and entropy, not lattice enthalpy alone. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: "Ionic and covalent bonding are completely different types of bonding." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: They are idealised extremes of a continuum described by electronegativity difference (bonding triangle).
items.markingKey: Arguments for: ionic bonding involves electron transfer and ions; covalent bonding involves shared pairs; they give very different properties. Arguments against: bonding is a continuum: most compounds have partial ionic and partial covalent character; polarisation of anions by small, highly charged cations gives covalent character (e.g. AlCl₃). Supported judgement: They are idealised extremes of a continuum described by electronegativity difference (bonding triangle). Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: "Systematic (IUPAC) names should completely replace traditional names such as “baking soda” or “ferric chloride”." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Systematic names should be used in science, while common names remain useful in everyday contexts – an example of language and knowledge (TOK).
items.markingKey: Arguments for: unambiguous international communication; encodes formula information. Arguments against: traditional names are familiar to the public and industry; systematic names can be long and confusing for non-specialists. Supported judgement: Systematic names should be used in science, while common names remain useful in everyday contexts – an example of language and knowledge (TOK).
